summary: This informational memo describes CAST-128, an existing encryption algorithm with a range of key sizes, offered to meet the need for an unencumbered cipher usable in cryptographic applications and protocols.

plainLanguage.summary: A secret way of scrambling messages, freely shared so anyone can use it.

subtitle: A freely-available encryption algorithm with a variable key size.

tldr.problem: The Internet community needs an unencumbered encryption algorithm suitable for a variety of cryptographic applications that does not rely on proprietary cipher designs.
tldr.mechanism: CAST-128 is a 12- or 16-round Feistel cipher with a 64-bit block size and variable key size up to 128 bits. It uses substitution boxes (S-boxes), rotation, and a mixture of XOR, addition and subtraction operations in its round function.
tldr.outcome: CAST-128 provides cryptographic strength suitable for general-purpose use and is available royalty-free for commercial and non-commercial use, making it available for incorporation into Internet protocols.

facts.label: Rounds
facts.value: 12 rounds for keys up to 80 bits; 16 rounds for larger keys

facts.label: S-boxes
facts.value: 8 substitution boxes with 256 entries each (1,024 bytes total)

facts.label: Subkeys generated
facts.value: 32 subkeys (16 masking keys and 16 rotation keys)

today: RFC 2144 is an Informational document and has not been obsoleted, so CAST-128 remains available for use as specified.

sections.title: What CAST-128 Is
sections.content:
RFC 2144 describes the CAST-128 encryption algorithm, a Feistel cipher that scrambles data to protect its confidentiality. It has desirable cryptographic properties including resistance to differential cryptanalysis, linear cryptanalysis, and related-key attacks. The cipher supports key sizes from 40 to 128 bits in 8-bit increments, using 12 rounds for keys up to 80 bits and 16 rounds for larger keys.

CAST-128 is freely available worldwide on a royalty-free basis for both commercial and non-commercial use, making it suitable for use throughout the Internet community.
sections.plainLanguage: CAST-128 is a machine for turning readable messages into gibberish. Only someone who knows the secret key can turn the gibberish back into a readable message.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
The CAST-128 algorithm works in four main steps. First, a 128-bit (or shorter, padded) key is processed to create 16 pairs of subkeys, one pair per round. Each pair consists of a 32-bit masking key and a 5-bit rotation key. Second, the 64-bit plaintext is split into left and right 32-bit halves. Third, the algorithm performs 16 (or 12) rounds of encryption, where each round applies an f function using one pair of subkeys. Fourth, the final left and right halves are swapped and concatenated to form the 64-bit ciphertext.

Decryption uses the same algorithm but applies the subkeys in reverse order. Three different f function types (Type 1, 2, and 3) are used in different rounds to increase security.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm splits your message in half, then does the same calculation 16 times, each time mixing the two halves together using part of the secret key. Each time, it uses a different way of mixing to make it harder to figure out.

sections.title: The Round Function
sections.content:
At the heart of each round is the f function, which processes data using one of three types depending on the round number. The input data is combined with a masking key, then rotated left by a number of positions specified by the rotation key. The result is split into four bytes, each of which indexes into one of four substitution boxes (S-boxes). The output values from the S-boxes are combined using XOR, addition, and subtraction operations to produce the round output.

The three function types vary their operations: Type 1 uses addition with the masking key and subtracts, Type 2 uses XOR with the masking key and XORs, and Type 3 uses subtraction with the masking key and adds. This variation prevents attackers from finding patterns.
sections.plainLanguage: Each round uses a special lookup table (the S-box) to transform the data in a way that is hard to reverse. Different rounds use different combinations of operations so an attacker cannot find a shortcut.

sections.title: Key Schedule and S-Boxes
sections.content:
CAST-128 uses eight 256-entry substitution boxes (S-boxes), each containing 1024 bytes of data. Four of these (S1 through S4) are used in the encryption rounds, while the other four (S5 through S8) are used only during key schedule generation. The key schedule algorithm processes the 128-bit key (with zero-padding if shorter) through a complex series of XOR and S-box operations to generate the 32 subkeys (K1 through K32). The first 16 subkeys are used as masking keys, and the next 16 are used as rotation keys.

The S-box design ensures good nonlinearity properties: each S-box has a minimum nonlinearity of 74 and a maximum entry of 2 in the difference distribution table, which resists cryptanalytic attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm uses special lookup tables that turn numbers into different numbers in a way that is hard to predict. The secret key is used to create the 32 tiny keys that are used one by one in each round.

sections.title: Security Analysis
sections.content:
CAST-128 appears to have cryptographic strength appropriate to its 128-bit key size. It offers resistance to differential and linear cryptanalysis through the use of rotation operations (which provide intrinsic immunity to linear attacks), a mixture of XOR, addition, and subtraction, and three variations of the round function. The cipher has no weak keys or semi-weak keys, and the S-boxes have favorable cryptographic properties.

Performance testing showed strong encryption and decryption speed of 3.3 megabytes per second on a 150 MHz Pentium processor. The algorithm has been analyzed in academic literature, and design and analysis details are available in the references.
sections.plainLanguage: Security experts have tested CAST-128 and found it to be strong. It works fast on computers and does not have any hidden weak points that would make it easier to crack.
